title: Can you structure these 8 pricing and product launch case questions in two minutes each?
description: 8 pricing and product launch case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Pricing and launch prompts. For pricing, build a range from three sides; for launches, pick the customer first. Give yourself two minutes per prompt, then open the model and look for what you missed.
body:
1. What price should a company charge for fast EV charging?

Show a model structure
  • Cost floor: Electricity, grid fees, equipment per kWh; Utilisation needed to break even
  • Customer value: Cost of charging at home vs on the road; Time saved, convenience
  • Competitors: Rivals' prices, subscriptions; Fuel cost per mile as a reference
  • Structure: Per kWh, per minute, subscription; Peak and off-peak

Where to start: Cost floor vs value ceiling: price sits between the two.

The trap: Copying rivals' prices without knowing your own cost and utilisation.

2. How should a snack brand launch a high-protein bar?

Show a model structure
  • Who: Target customers and their need; Size of the segment
  • What: Product, flavours, pack sizes; Price vs rivals
  • Where and how: Channels: supermarkets, gyms, online; Marketing and sampling
  • Economics and risks: Volume to break even; Cannibalisation of our other bars

Where to start: Who: a launch without a clear target customer spreads money thin.

The trap: Starting with advertising before choosing the customer and the channel.

3. Should a supermarket launch a premium own-label range?

Show a model structure
  • Customer demand: Shoppers buying premium brands; Willingness to trust our brand
  • Economics: Margin vs branded products; Volume needed to cover development
  • Suppliers: Who can make it at quality; Reaction of big brands
  • Cannibalisation: Sales taken from our standard own-label; Net margin gained

Where to start: Margin vs branded: premium own-label usually earns more per item.

The trap: Ignoring how the big brands might react, such as cutting promotions.

4. Should a business school launch a fully online MBA?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: Students who can't study on campus; Price they would pay
  • Competition: Other online MBAs and their prices; Our brand vs theirs
  • Economics: Development and teaching cost; Students needed to break even
  • Cannibalisation and brand: Cannibalising our campus MBA; Perceived quality and rankings

Where to start: Cannibalisation of the campus MBA, often the school's flagship programme.

The trap: Assuming online students are all new.

5. Should an electronics retailer introduce a price-match guarantee?

Show a model structure
  • Customer impact: Extra sales from confidence; Share of customers who would claim
  • Cost: Margin given up on matched sales; Admin to check claims
  • Competitor response: Rivals matching back, price war; Online-only rivals
  • Rules: Which rivals and products; In-store vs online

Where to start: Cost: how many sales would be matched, and at what discount.

The trap: Assuming only a few customers will claim.

6. Should a design-software company add a free plan?

Show a model structure
  • Acquisition: New users attracted; Conversion from free to paid
  • Cannibalisation: Paying users moving down; What the free plan leaves out
  • Costs: Hosting and support for free users; Fraud and abuse
  • Competition: Rivals' free plans; How customers choose a tool

Where to start: Conversion from free to paid vs paying users who downgrade.

The trap: Counting sign-ups as success.

7. Should a streaming service launch a cheaper plan with ads?

Show a model structure
  • New subscribers: People who find the full price too high; Win-back of those who left
  • Downgrades: Current subscribers switching to cheaper plan; Revenue lost per switch
  • Ad revenue: Ads per hour, price advertisers pay; Viewer experience
  • Capability: Ad sales team, technology; Content rights for ads

Where to start: Downgrades: ad revenue must make up for subscribers who switch down.

The trap: Counting only the new subscribers.

8. How should an insurer launch weather insurance for small farmers in Kenya?

Show a model structure
  • Farmers' need: Losses from drought and floods; What they can afford
  • Product design: Payouts based on rainfall data; Price and cover
  • Distribution: Mobile money, co-operatives, seed sellers; Bundling with loans
  • Economics and risk: Claims in a bad year; Reinsurance, government support

Where to start: Distribution: reaching small farmers cheaply decides whether it works.

The trap: Designing a product farmers can't pay for or reach.
